title: Clearview Dental Group: testing a collections change with confidence levels, significance tests and associations
participant_role: Financial analyst in the accounting department of a dental practice
judge_role: Practice administrator of Clearview Dental Group, who must recommend a collections change to the dentist partners

difficulty.rationale: Interpret t test, confidence intervals and chi-square output; AP Statistics level.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a financial analyst in the accounting department of CLEARVIEW DENTAL GROUP, a multi office dental practice. The practice administrator (judge) has asked you to review the results of a collections test and recommend what the practice should do next.

CLEARVIEW DENTAL GROUP bills about $500,000 a month, or about $16,667 a day. After insurance pays its share, patients currently take an average of 24 days to pay their balances, and the practice administrator (judge) believes slow collections are squeezing cash. For three months the billing office ran a test: 60 patients received text message payment reminders with a link to pay online, and 60 patients received the usual mailed letters. The billing office also tracked which patients paid more than 30 days late.

The accounting department entered the results into statistical software. The output is shown below along with the cost of each type of reminder.

[Exhibit A: Reminder test results: see exhibits]

[Exhibit B: Payer type and late payment: see exhibits]

The practice administrator (judge) must present a recommendation to the dentist partners next week and wants to understand what the statistics really prove, how confident the practice can be and what the results mean for cash.

You must:
- Explain how to select a confidence level for the practice's tests
- Determine whether the text reminders made a meaningful difference in collection time
- Determine whether payer type is associated with paying late
- Draw preliminary conclusions from the statistical results, including the effect on cash
- Explain the limits of the test and what should happen next

You will present the information to the practice administrator (judge) in a role-play to take place in the practice administrator's office. The practice administrator (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the practice administrator's (judge's) questions, the practice administrator (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Explain how to select a confidence level for the practice's tests
Determine whether the text reminders made a meaningful difference in collection time
Determine whether payer type is associated with paying late
Draw preliminary conclusions from the statistical results, including the effect on cash
Explain the limits of the test and what should happen next

exhibits.title: Exhibit A: Reminder test results (two sample t test)
Exhibit B: Payer type and late payment (over 30 days)

performance_indicators: Use statistical data inferences to draw preliminary conclusions

pi_links.text: Use statistical data inferences to draw preliminary conclusions

century_skills: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking
Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems
Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity
judge_questions: The 99% interval is wider. Does that mean the result is weaker?
Could we just switch everyone to texts and skip more testing?

solution.overview: A strong answer chooses the 95% confidence level as the business standard (99% for costly or risky decisions), shows that text reminders cut collection time by 6 days with a result that is both statistically significant (p < 0.001, interval excludes 0) and practically meaningful, and shows that self pay patients are more likely to pay late (35% vs 20%, p = 0.018). The presenter converts the 6 days into about $100,000 of cash freed, notes texts also save $0.70 per reminder, recommends adopting texts and targeting self pay patients, and explains the limits of a 3 month, 120 patient test.

answer: The confidence level is how sure we want to be before we act on a result
95% is the common business standard: about a 5% chance of a false alarm
Use 99% when a wrong decision would be costly or risky; it requires stronger evidence
Choose the level before looking at the results so the test is fair
Text group paid in 18 days on average versus 24 days for letters: a 6 day difference
p value less than 0.001 is far below 0.05, so the difference is statistically significant
Both confidence intervals (3.4 to 8.6 and 2.6 to 9.4 days) are above 0, so the difference is real at 95% and 99%
Six days is also practically meaningful for cash flow, not just a statistical result

by_task.task: Association between payer type and late payment
answer: Self pay patients paid late 35% of the time versus 20% for insured patients
Chi square p value 0.018 is below 0.05, so payer type is associated with late payment at the 95% level
It would not pass at the 99% level (0.018 is above 0.01), so the evidence is good but not overwhelming
Association is not causation: balance size or income may explain why self pay patients pay later
Collecting 6 days faster frees about 6 x $16,667 = about $100,000 of cash
Texts are also cheaper: $0.75 minus $0.05 = $0.70 saved per reminder
Adopt text reminders with an online payment link
Target self pay patients with payment plans or a card on file
Only 3 months of data, so seasonal patterns may be missed
Only 120 patients; a larger sample gives more reliable results
Patients should be randomly assigned to each group so the groups are alike
Rerun or keep monitoring the results after the rollout to confirm them

calculations.label: Difference in collection time
steps: Letter group mean 24 days minus text group mean 18 days = 6 days
95% confidence interval 3.4 to 8.6 days does not include 0
99% confidence interval 2.6 to 9.4 days does not include 0

calculations.label: Reminder cost savings
steps: Letter $0.75 minus text $0.05 = $0.70 saved per reminder

calculations.label: Late payment rates by payer type
steps: Chi square p value 0.018 < 0.05, so the association is significant at 95%

judge_question_answers.question: The 99% interval is wider. Does that mean the result is weaker?
answer: No: the 99% interval is wider because we are demanding more certainty, not because the evidence is weaker
The same data and the same 6 day difference produce both intervals
Even the wider 99% interval stays above 0, which shows the result is strong
Think of it as a wider net: to be more sure you catch the true value, the net must be bigger

judge_question_answers.question: Could we just switch everyone to texts and skip more testing?
answer: The evidence is strong enough to roll texts out, and texts are cheaper, so the risk is low
But keep measuring days to collect after the switch to confirm the result holds
Keep letters for patients without a mobile phone or who opt out of texts
Watch for problems such as texts going to wrong numbers or privacy rules for patient messages

key_concepts.definition: How sure we want to be that a result is not due to chance, commonly 95% in business and 99% for high stakes decisions.
The chance of seeing a result this large if there were really no difference. A p value below 0.05 is statistically significant at the 95% level.
A range that likely contains the true difference. If the interval does not include 0, the difference is statistically significant.
A test that compares the means of two groups to see whether the difference between them is real or due to chance.
A test that checks whether two categories, such as payer type and late payment, are associated.
A result can be real (statistically significant) but too small to matter. A meaningful difference is both real and large enough to affect decisions.
Two things occurring together does not prove one causes the other. Other factors may explain the link.
Placing subjects into test groups by chance so the groups are alike and the test is fair.
The number of observations in a test. Larger samples give more reliable conclusions.
The average number of days customers take to pay. Fewer days means cash comes in sooner.

notes: ICDC level because students must interpret p values, two confidence intervals and a chi square result, then turn them into a cash impact and a cautious recommendation. Watch for students who think a wider 99% interval means a weaker result, who treat the payer type association as proof of cause, or who forget to state the test's limits.

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the confidence level is how sure the practice wants to be before acting, recommends 95% as the business standard (about a 5% chance of a false alarm), uses 99% for costly or risky decisions, and stresses choosing the level before looking at the results.
criteria.meets: Selects 95% as the standard confidence level and explains that 99% is used when a wrong decision would be costly or risky.
criteria.below: Names a confidence level without explaining why, or cannot explain the tradeoff between 95% and 99%.
criteria.little: Does not select a confidence level, or confuses the confidence level with the p value.

criteria.exceeds: Uses the t test output to show a definite relationship between reminder type and collection time: a p value below 0.001 is far below 0.05, and both the 95% interval (3.4 to 8.6 days) and the 99% interval (2.6 to 9.4 days) stay above 0, so the result holds at either confidence level.
criteria.meets: States that the p value below 0.001 and confidence intervals that exclude 0 show text reminders are related to faster collection.
criteria.below: Mentions the p value or an interval but cannot explain what it proves, or thinks the wider 99% interval weakens the result.
criteria.little: Does not interpret the t test results, or concludes there is no relationship.

criteria.exceeds: Shows self pay patients paid late 35% of the time versus 20% for insured patients, explains the chi square p value of 0.018 is significant at 95% but not at 99% (above 0.01), and cautions that association is not causation (balance size or income may explain it).
criteria.meets: States self pay patients are late 35% of the time versus 20% for insured patients and that the p value of 0.018 shows an association at the 95% level.
criteria.below: Notes the late payment difference but cannot interpret the 0.018 p value, or treats the association as proof that being self pay causes late payment.
criteria.little: Does not address the payer type data, or concludes there is no association.

criteria.exceeds: Shows the text group paid in 18 days versus 24 days, a 6 day difference that is both statistically significant and practically meaningful, because it frees about $100,000 of cash (6 x $16,667) and each text saves $0.70 over a letter.
criteria.meets: Identifies the 6 day difference (18 versus 24 days) as statistically significant and meaningful for cash flow.
criteria.below: States the 6 day difference but does not explain whether it is significant or why it matters in practice.
criteria.little: Does not compare the two groups, or misreads the difference.

items.label: Use statistical data inferences to draw preliminary conclusions

criteria.exceeds: Recommends adopting text reminders with an online payment link and targeting self pay patients with payment plans or a card on file, while explaining the limits (only 3 months and 120 patients, need for random assignment) and the need to keep monitoring after rollout.
criteria.meets: Recommends adopting text reminders, citing the about $100,000 of cash freed, and names at least one limit of the test.
criteria.below: Draws a conclusion without the cash effect, or ignores the limits of a small 3 month test.
criteria.little: Draws no conclusion, or draws conclusions the data do not support.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the statistical results to cash flow, cost savings and collection strategy, and separates statistical significance from practical importance and association from causation.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the software output to the conclusions about texts and payer type.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or overstates what the statistics prove.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the administrator a clear recommendation for the partners (roll out texts, target self pay patients) along with a plan to confirm the results with ongoing monitoring.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation to adopt text reminders.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.

criteria.exceeds: Explains p values, confidence intervals and the chi square result in plain language the administrator can repeat to the dentist partners, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the statistical results and recommendation clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on statistical jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Turns the statistics into something memorable, such as expressing the 6 days as about $100,000 of cash, and adds useful ideas like payment plans or a card on file for self pay patients.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the results easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions confidently: the 99% interval is wider because it demands more certainty from the same data, and since it still stays above 0 the result is strong; and texts can be rolled out because the evidence is strong and texts are cheaper, while keeping letters for patients without phones, watching privacy rules and measuring days to collect after the switch.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that a wider 99% interval does not mean a weaker result and that results should be monitored after switching.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says the wider 99% interval means the result is weaker.

key_points: Use 95% as the standard confidence level; use 99% when a wrong decision would be costly or risky, and choose it before seeing the results
Texts cut collection time from 24 to 18 days, a 6 day difference with p below 0.001
Both confidence intervals (3.4 to 8.6 and 2.6 to 9.4 days) exclude 0, so the difference is real at 95% and 99%
Collecting 6 days faster frees about 6 x $16,667 = about $100,000 of cash, and texts save $0.70 per reminder
Self pay patients pay late 35% of the time versus 20% for insured; p = 0.018 is significant at 95% but not at 99%
Limits: only 3 months and 120 patients, groups should be randomly assigned, and results should be monitored after rollout
